segments.text: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere; climate is the long-term pattern and variability of weather conditions. This unit explains why temperature, pressure, winds and rainfall differ across the world.
Think of the atmosphere as an energy-and-water system. Solar energy is received unevenly, air moves to redistribute heat, water circulates, and local factors modify the result.

items.text: Elements and factors of climate

: Elements include temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, cloud and precipitation. Major controls include latitude, altitude, distance from sea, ocean currents, relief, prevailing winds and land cover.
Structure and composition of atmosphere

: The atmosphere is mainly nitrogen and oxygen with smaller amounts of other gases and variable water vapour. Temperature changes with height define layers such as the troposphere and stratosphere; most everyday weather occurs in the troposphere.
Insolation and temperature

: Insolation is incoming solar radiation. Its amount varies with sun angle, day length, cloud and surface characteristics. Temperature also depends on heat transfer, altitude, continentality and ocean influence.
Pressure belts
: Unequal heating and Earth’s rotation contribute to broad pressure zones such as equatorial low pressure, subtropical highs, subpolar lows and polar highs. These belts shift seasonally.
Heat budget
: Earth’s heat budget describes the balance among incoming solar energy, reflection and outgoing terrestrial radiation. Regional imbalance drives atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
Planetary, monsoon and local winds

: Global winds include trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies. Monsoons involve seasonal reversal or major seasonal change in wind linked with land-sea heating and atmospheric circulation. Local winds develop from smaller-scale temperature and pressure differences.
Air masses and fronts
: An air mass is a large body of air with broadly similar temperature and moisture characteristics. Fronts are boundaries between contrasting air masses and can produce clouds, rain and storms.
Hydrological cycle
: Water moves through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, groundwater flow and runoff. It links atmosphere, land, oceans and living systems.
Condensation and precipitation

: Cooling air to saturation can produce dew, fog or clouds. Precipitation forms through processes that allow droplets or ice particles to grow enough to fall. Major rainfall mechanisms include convectional, orographic and frontal/cyclonic uplift.
Global distribution of precipitation
: Rainfall is influenced by circulation belts, monsoons, oceans, relief, latitude and storm tracks. Windward mountain slopes are often wetter than leeward rain-shadow areas.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

items.text: Composition

: Dry air is dominated by nitrogen and oxygen, with smaller proportions of argon, carbon dioxide and other gases. Water vapour is highly variable and is essential to clouds, precipitation and the greenhouse effect.
Troposphere
: Most weather occurs in the troposphere, where temperature generally decreases with height because the atmosphere is heated mainly from Earth's surface and because rising air expands and cools.
Stratosphere
: Temperature increases with height in much of the stratosphere because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation. The stable structure limits vertical mixing compared with the troposphere.
Higher layers
: The mesosphere and thermosphere have different thermal patterns and contain very thin air. For ordinary climate analysis, the troposphere and lower stratosphere are most important.

blocks.text: Insolation, albedo and the heat budget

items.text: Solar angle
: Low-latitude surfaces receive more concentrated solar energy because rays strike more directly. Seasonal changes in sun angle and day length arise from Earth's axial tilt and revolution.
Albedo
: Bright surfaces reflect a larger proportion of incoming shortwave radiation, while darker surfaces absorb more. Snow and ice therefore have important feedback effects in the climate system.
Greenhouse effect

: Earth's surface absorbs solar energy and emits longwave radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit some outgoing infrared radiation, keeping the lower atmosphere warmer than it would otherwise be. Human-caused increases in greenhouse gases strengthen this natural effect.
Regional imbalance
: Tropical regions receive a net surplus of energy while high latitudes lose more than they gain. Atmospheric and oceanic circulation redistribute heat and reduce the contrast.
Pressure-gradient force
: Air accelerates from relatively high toward relatively low pressure. The stronger the pressure gradient, the stronger the tendency for wind to accelerate.
Coriolis effect

: Earth's rotation deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere. The Coriolis effect changes direction, not the existence of the original pressure force.
Friction
: Near the surface, friction slows wind and weakens Coriolis deflection, allowing air to cross isobars more directly toward low pressure.
Global cells

: The Hadley, Ferrel and polar circulation cells are idealized components of the general circulation. They help explain trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies and major pressure belts, but real circulation shifts seasonally and is modified by continents and topography.
Jet streams
: Fast upper-level winds near strong horizontal temperature gradients help steer weather systems and influence storm tracks.

blocks.text: Air masses, fronts and mid-latitude weather

items.text: Air mass

: An air mass forms over a source region and acquires broad temperature and moisture characteristics. Maritime sources tend to be moister than continental sources; tropical sources are warmer than polar sources.
Front
: A front is a transition zone between contrasting air masses. Warm, cold, stationary and occluded fronts produce different patterns of uplift, cloud and precipitation.
Cyclones

: Mid-latitude cyclones develop around low-pressure systems and fronts, drawing energy from strong horizontal temperature contrasts. Their passage often produces systematic changes in wind, pressure, cloud and precipitation.
Anticyclones
: High-pressure systems are associated with subsiding air, which suppresses cloud formation in many conditions. Persistent highs can therefore contribute to dry spells or heat events.
Humidity

: Absolute measures describe water vapour content, while relative humidity compares actual vapour with the maximum possible at the same temperature. Relative humidity can change because temperature changes even when water vapour content stays constant.
Adiabatic cooling

: Rising air expands in lower pressure and cools without necessarily exchanging heat with its surroundings. Cooling toward saturation promotes condensation if condensation nuclei and sufficient moisture are present.
Convectional rain
: Strong surface heating can make air buoyant. Rising moist air cools, condenses and may produce showers or thunderstorms.
Orographic rain
: Moist air forced over high ground cools and can produce windward precipitation. Descending air on the leeward side warms and dries, creating a rain-shadow tendency.
Frontal/cyclonic rain
: Convergence and frontal uplift force air upward over broad areas, often producing widespread precipitation.
Monsoon concept

: A monsoon is a seasonal circulation system with major wind reversal or directional change tied to seasonal heating, pressure patterns and the migration of rain-bearing circulation. The South Asian monsoon is not explained by land-sea contrast alone; upper-air circulation, the Tibetan Plateau, ocean conditions and intraseasonal variability also matter.
Sea and land breezes
: Coasts can develop daily wind reversals because land heats and cools faster than water. Sea breezes usually develop during daytime heating; land breezes are more likely at night.
Mountain and valley winds
: Slope heating by day can drive upslope or valley winds, while nighttime radiative cooling encourages downslope drainage of denser air.

blocks.text: Weather versus climate and why the distinction matters

segments.text: Weather refers to short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes long-term statistical patterns including averages, variability and extremes. A single cold day cannot disprove a warming climate, just as one heatwave cannot by itself establish a long-term trend. Climate analysis depends on records across many years and on spatially broad evidence.
Reading the flow: each step creates the conditions for the next; the arrows show sequence or influence, not inevitability unless the text explicitly says so.

rows: Avoid this error Do not write that air “simply moves from hot to cold.” Wind is driven by pressure-gradient forces and modified by rotation, friction and circulation patterns.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Start with climate elements and controls, explain atmosphere and energy balance, then pressure/winds, air masses/fronts and the water cycle, ending with rainfall types and global distribution.
• Federal Public Service Commission, Revised Scheme and Syllabus for CSS Competitive Examination (CE-2016 and onwards).
• NOAA educational resources on atmosphere, circulation and weather; standard physical-geography texts.
• Weather is short-term atmospheric condition; climate concerns long-term patterns.
• Unequal solar heating is a fundamental driver of circulation.
• Winds move from pressure differences but are deflected by Earth’s rotation and affected by friction.
• The hydrological cycle continually transfers water among atmosphere, land and oceans.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
